title: Building Coalitions
subtitle: Creating Alliances for Change
description: Build and maintain coalitions to drive large-scale digital transformation initiatives.
targetAudience: DPI advisors, government IT directors, policy coordinators

content.overview: Coalitions are networks of organizations and stakeholders united around a common objective. In digital public infrastructure contexts, coalitions multiply your influence and distribute risk. A single champion can be isolated or dismissed; a coalition of ministers, civil society, and private sector players becomes institutional. This module explores why coalitions matter, how they create asymmetric advantage, and the foundational logic behind coalition building.

keyPoints.title: Coalition as Force Multiplier
keyPoints.description: One minister requesting digital transformation can be overruled. Five ministers, two civil society organizations, and three private sector leaders demanding interoperability create institutional inevitability. Coalitions transform from 'nice to have' to 'necessary to acknowledge.' The coalition effect multiplies credibility by distributing the ask across multiple legitimate voices.

keyPoints.title: Risk Distribution and Institutional Protection
keyPoints.description: When a single government agency champions DPI, bureaucratic infighting, budget cuts, or leadership changes can derail the entire initiative. Coalitions distribute this risk across multiple institutions. If one partner faces opposition, others can amplify the message. This institutional redundancy creates resilience against political volatility.

keyPoints.title: Access and Legitimacy Expansion
keyPoints.description: A government DPI team reaches treasury and ministry officials. Adding civil society partners reaches grassroots communities and NGO networks. Adding private sector reaches businesses and digital platforms. The coalition's combined network is exponentially larger than any single member. Each partner brings unique access and legitimacy in their domain.

keyPoints.title: Diverse Perspective Integration
keyPoints.description: A treasury economist sees budget implications. A civil society advocate sees equity concerns. A private sector partner sees scalability and technology options. These diverse perspectives prevent blind spots, improve policy design, and increase implementation viability. Coalition diversity forces rigor and completeness of thinking.

content.keyInsight: Coalitions are not optional add-ons to digital transformation—they are structural necessities. In complex, multi-stakeholder environments like government digital transformation, change requires collective action. Coalitions convert individual influence into institutional inevitability, distribute risk across multiple bodies, and integrate perspectives necessary for robust, equitable solutions.

exercises.prompt: Consider a recent DPI initiative in your context. What single institution championed it? What would have changed if it had been championed by a coalition of 4-5 different institutions?
Map one digital transformation failure you've observed. To what extent was isolation from coalition partners a contributing factor? What coalition might have prevented this failure?

content.overview: Before building a coalition, you must map stakeholders systematically. Not all stakeholders should be coalition members—some are blockers, some are supporters, some are neutral. This module teaches the mechanics of stakeholder mapping specifically for coalition building: identifying who needs to be included, understanding their interests, assessing their power and influence, and determining their optimal role in the coalition structure.

keyPoints.title: Stakeholder Categories and Roles
keyPoints.description: Core Coalition Members: Organizations with direct stake in outcomes and capacity to contribute resources (budget, people, convening power). Example: In India's UPI coalition, RBI, NPCI, major banks, and ICICI Bank were core members. Champions: High-visibility individuals who lend credibility and convening power. Example: A finance minister publicly backing payments interoperability. Supporting Organizations: Organizations that benefit but require less management. Example: Merchant associations supporting UPI expansion. Blockers: Organizations with veto power or resources to undermine. Example: Incumbent financial institutions initially concerned about disruption. Your coalition strategy must explicitly place each stakeholder in one of these roles.

keyPoints.title: Power-Interest Matrix for Coalition Composition
keyPoints.description: Plot stakeholders on a two-axis matrix: horizontal axis shows their interest in the initiative (low to high), vertical axis shows their power/influence (low to high). High power + high interest: Must be coalition members. Example: Ministry of Finance for a digital economy initiative. High power + low interest: Make allies early or manage risks. Example: Defense Ministry in a civilian digital identity initiative. Low power + high interest: Support and enable participation. Example: Women's groups in a digital inclusion coalition. Low power + low interest: Monitor but don't prioritize. This mapping prevents wasting coalition time on low-impact stakeholders while ensuring high-influence players are strategically engaged.

keyPoints.title: Interest-Conflict Mapping
keyPoints.description: Even within a coalition, stakeholders have different interests. A payments system coalition includes: banks (interest in profitability), government (interest in financial inclusion), merchants (interest in cost reduction), consumers (interest in convenience and security). These interests sometimes align and sometimes conflict. Explicitly map where interests align (areas for coalition agreement) and where they diverge (areas requiring negotiation or compartmentalization). Example: In India's UPI coalition, banks initially worried about revenue loss from reduced check clearing. Government prioritized financial inclusion. The coalition addressed both by (1) accelerating merchant UPI adoption to drive volume, (2) allowing banks to monetize through premium services. Interest mapping enabled this simultaneous addressing of different concerns.

keyPoints.title: Influence Network Analysis
keyPoints.description: In government contexts, formal power (the org chart) and actual influence (who people listen to) differ significantly. A permanent secretary may have less influence than a respected technical expert. A CEO may have less influence on government policy than a civil society leader with media relationships. Map influence networks by asking: 'Who influences your boss? Who influences budget decisions? Whose views matter in your field?' Identify influence brokers—people trusted across multiple constituencies. These people become coalition anchors. Example: In a digital identity coalition, an economist with credibility in both government and think tanks can bridge the trust gap between suspicious civil libertarians and efficiency-focused civil servants.

content.keyInsight: Coalition composition determines success or failure. Systematic stakeholder mapping prevents two critical errors: including blockers who slow progress, or excluding necessary partners who later become obstacles. A well-mapped coalition includes core members with complementary resources and influence, manages potential blockers early, and explicitly accounts for competing interests within the coalition.

exercises.prompt: Select a digital transformation initiative in your context. Create a stakeholder map: (1) List at least 12 stakeholders. (2) Place each on a power-interest matrix. (3) Categorize as core member, champion, supporter, or blocker. (4) Identify 2-3 potential conflicts between stakeholder interests.

Examine an actual coalition in your field (e.g., a real DPI initiative or payments system rollout). Who were the core members? Who was excluded? Who later became blockers? Could better stakeholder mapping have prevented those blockers?

content.overview: Building the initial coalition requires sequencing and strategic entry points. You cannot recruit everyone simultaneously; you must sequence recruitment to create momentum and credibility. This module teaches the mechanics: identifying the anchor organization, recruiting founding members, managing the founding coalition meeting, and establishing coalition identity and norms.

keyPoints.title: Anchor Organization and First Followers
keyPoints.description: Every successful coalition starts with an anchor—an organization with enough institutional resources, credibility, and alignment to convene others. In government contexts, the anchor is typically a powerful ministry or state institution. India's UPI was anchored by the Reserve Bank of India, which had regulatory authority and trust across the financial system. The coalition then recruits 'first followers'—2-3 organizations aligned with the anchor's vision and credible enough to attract others. First followers solve the cold-start problem: they validate that the coalition is serious and real. Recruit founding members through direct outreach, not open calls. Example: In building a civil registration coalition, your anchor (perhaps the Interior Ministry) reaches out to specific health ministries, state governments, and civil society leaders—not through a press release but through personal convenings.

keyPoints.title: Founding Coalition Meeting Design
keyPoints.description: The first coalition meeting sets norms for all future interactions. A poorly designed founding meeting creates bad habits that plague the coalition throughout its life. A well-designed meeting clarifies: (1) Coalition purpose—specifically, not vaguely. Not 'improve digital systems' but 'interoperate 12 government databases to reduce citizen wait times from 45 days to 5 days.' (2) Each member's specific role and contribution. Not 'the finance ministry will support' but 'the finance ministry will allocate 2 billion rupees over 18 months and assign a joint secretary to the coalition steering committee.' (3) Governance structure and decision-making processes. Who has veto power? How are disputes resolved? (4) Timeline and milestones. When does the coalition aim to deliver? What are the intermediate checkpoints? Design the founding meeting around these four elements. Include a 'moment of commitment'—ideally a signed letter or public statement where each founding member formally commits to coalition membership.

keyPoints.title: Coalition Charter and Identity
keyPoints.description: Coalitions need visible identity separate from any single member. This identity makes the coalition feel 'real' to external audiences and creates psychological investment among members. Elements of coalition identity: (1) Coalition name that captures purpose. Example: 'India Stack Operators Coalition' vs. the vague 'Digital Infrastructure Partnership.' (2) Logo or visual mark. (3) Regular meeting schedule and venue—even a virtual one conveys continuity. (4) Charter document that establishes principles. Example: 'We commit to interoperability standards that prioritize financial inclusion over individual institutional profit.' (5) Shared communication—a newsletter or platform where coalition announcements go. (6) Coalition spokesperson or rotating spokesperson arrangement. This identity simultaneously signals external credibility and creates internal cohesion.

keyPoints.title: Managing Early Skeptics and Uncommitted Partners
keyPoints.description: Not every recruited organization will commit fully to the founding coalition. Some will attend meetings but remain noncommittal. Others will commit to principles but not to specific resource contributions. This is normal. Rather than treating skeptics as failures, use the founding phase to convert skeptics into committed members or strategic supporters. Offer graduated commitment levels: (1) Steering committee member—highest commitment, includes attending monthly meetings and contributing resources. (2) Working group member—medium commitment, focused on specific technical or policy tasks. (3) Observer or advisor—light commitment, provides input without ongoing obligations. (4) Aligned organization—lowest commitment, publicly supports coalition but not formally part of governance. This graduated structure allows organizations to join at their comfort level and upgrade commitment as trust builds. Example: When India's open data coalition was forming, some civil society organizations started as observers, then joined specific working groups, then eventually became steering committee members as they saw value and reduced risk.

content.keyInsight: Building a coalition begins with identifying an anchor organization credible enough to convene others. Early success depends on recruiting first followers who validate the coalition's credibility, designing a founding meeting that clarifies purpose and contributions, and establishing visible coalition identity. Offer graduated commitment levels to manage skeptics and create pathways for later escalation of involvement.

exercises.prompt: Design a founding coalition meeting for a DPI initiative in your context. Specify: (1) Who is the anchor organization and why? (2) Who are the first 3-5 followers and why are they strategically important? (3) What are the four key agenda items for the founding meeting? (4) What specific commitment statements will you seek from each founding member?

Imagine you are convening a data interoperability coalition. A large ministry attends the meeting but remains noncommittal. Draft a follow-up conversation where you offer a graduated commitment path that moves them from observer to active participant.

content.overview: Coalition members join for different reasons. A ministry joins for institutional credit. A civil society organization joins to ensure equity considerations. A private company joins for market opportunity. A state government joins to improve service delivery. These diverse interests can be fuel for innovation or sources of constant conflict. This module teaches the craft of aligning interests: identifying shared value, managing competing interests, negotiating coalition agreements, and using structure to accommodate diversity.

keyPoints.title: Shared Value Identification and Articulation
keyPoints.description: The coalition's public messaging focuses on shared value—the outcome that genuinely benefits all members. Example: A digital identity coalition might have shared value as 'secure, accessible identity for all citizens.' This is genuinely valuable to government (reduces fraud, improves targeting), to civil society (enables inclusion), and to private sector (enables efficient service delivery). Shared value is not a compromise where everyone gets 50% of what they want. It is identifying the outcome where all members genuinely benefit, even if they benefit differently. Government benefits from reduced fraud. Civil society benefits from inclusion. Private sector benefits from lower transaction costs. These are different benefits, but they all flow from the same outcome: secure, accessible identity. Explicitly articulate this shared value in coalition messaging. When conflicts arise, return to shared value: 'How do we achieve secure, accessible identity in a way that serves government's fraud-reduction needs, civil society's inclusion agenda, and private sector's efficiency needs?' This reframes conflicts as problem-solving rather than win-lose bargaining.

keyPoints.title: Interest Mapping and Negotiation
keyPoints.description: Beyond shared value, coalition members have specific, sometimes competing interests. A coalition agreement must acknowledge and negotiate these interests explicitly. Create an 'interest matrix' for each major coalition decision: list stakeholders vertically and potential options horizontally. For each combination, assess impact: positive, neutral, or negative. Example: If deciding whether to make a digital identity system interoperable with private sector platforms, the matrix might look like: Government agency (positive—extends reach without cost), Civil society (negative—privacy concerns), Private sector (positive—access to verified identity). This matrix makes conflicts visible. The coalition then negotiates: Can privacy concerns be addressed through stronger data governance? Can civil society's concerns be incorporated into the interoperability rules? Sometimes the answer is 'no' and the coalition decides one interest takes priority. Example: In India's UPI coalition, incumbent banks' interest in protecting branch-based revenue had to yield to the coalition's interest in promoting digital payments. But the coalition negotiated that banks could offer premium services beyond basic UPI, allowing banks to maintain some revenue opportunity. This was negotiated interest accommodation, not win-lose conflict.

keyPoints.title: Coalition Agreement and Written Commitments
keyPoints.description: Coalitions need written, specific agreements. Verbal understanding is insufficient; different parties will interpret ambiguous language differently. A coalition agreement should specify: (1) Coalition objective and success criteria. How will the coalition know it succeeded? (2) Each member's specific contributions. Not 'Bank A will support the initiative' but 'Bank A will connect 500 of its branches to the system by month 6, allocate 2 FTEs to the technical working group, and allocate 200,000 rupees to the marketing campaign.' (3) Governance structure and decision-making rules. Do decisions require consensus, majority vote, or steering committee approval? (4) Dispute resolution process. If members disagree, how is conflict resolved? (5) Timeline and milestones. (6) Exit conditions. Under what circumstances can a member leave? What are the consequences? (7) Confidentiality and information-sharing rules. (8) How the coalition will communicate publicly. A detailed coalition agreement reduces misunderstanding and creates clear expectations. Example: The Global Digital Compact (a real multi-stakeholder coalition) has extensive agreements specifying each stakeholder group's commitments and roles.

keyPoints.title: Structural Accommodation of Diverse Interests
keyPoints.description: Sometimes conflicts cannot be resolved through shared value or negotiation. In these cases, structure the coalition to accommodate both interests. Example: A government transparency initiative coalition includes civil society organizations wanting maximum data release and government agencies concerned about security and privacy. Rather than resolving this as a binary choice, the coalition might structure as: (1) Core working group for data strategy—includes both advocates and cautious agencies, working to find balanced approach. (2) Security subgroup for government and technical experts—addresses security concerns in depth. (3) Transparency subgroup for civil society and advocates—develops implementation mechanisms for maximum appropriate release. (4) Governance group that integrates outputs. This structure acknowledges that both interests are legitimate and creates space for each to do deep work while integrating at the whole-coalition level. Another structural approach: tiered rollout. Launch the initiative in a conservative way that satisfies skeptics (slower rollout, more safeguards), with planned expansion to more aggressive versions. Example: India's Aadhaar program initially focused on financial inclusion, which satisfied government's efficiency interest. Over time, it expanded to other services, which satisfied civil society's access interest. The staged rollout allowed both interests to be accommodated over time rather than resolved immediately.

content.keyInsight: Coalition members' diverse interests are not obstacles to manage; they are sources of robustness. Diverse interests mean diverse expertise, perspectives, and constituencies. Successfully align interests by: identifying shared value that benefits all members even if differently; explicitly negotiating competing interests rather than hoping they'll disappear; codifying agreements in writing; and using coalition structure to accommodate interests that cannot be fully reconciled.

exercises.prompt: Select a multi-stakeholder DPI initiative. Map the interests of 4-5 key stakeholders on a shared value/competing interests matrix. (1) What is the shared value that unites them? (2) Where do interests genuinely conflict? (3) How would you negotiate or structurally accommodate these conflicts?

You are convening a coalition for a government data exchange platform. Government wants maximum data sharing. Civil society wants strong privacy safeguards. Private sector wants data access to build services. Draft a coalition agreement that specifies: (1) shared value, (2) each stakeholder's specific contribution, (3) governance structure for ongoing interest negotiation, (4) dispute resolution process.

content.overview: A coalition is not a single organization; it is a network of independent organizations coordinating toward shared objectives. Governance structures must reflect this reality. This module covers the mechanics of coalition governance: decision-making structures, roles and responsibilities, meeting cadence and formats, communication channels, and conflict resolution.

keyPoints.title: Decision-Making Structures
keyPoints.description: Coalition governance requires multiple layers of decision-making. (1) Steering Committee: Core coalition members (typically 8-12 organizations) who set direction, approve major decisions, allocate resources, and represent coalition externally. Meets monthly or quarterly. Examples of committees: steering committee includes ministry heads, CSO directors, private sector CTOs. (2) Working Groups: Task-focused groups organized around specific initiatives (technical integration, policy development, communications, implementation). Each working group includes 4-10 people from different coalition members. Meets 2-4 times per month. (3) Technical Advisory Group: For digital initiatives, technical experts from member organizations who provide specialized input on technical standards, architecture, security. Meets monthly. (4) Operational Team: A small team (typically 2-4 people from the anchor organization) managing day-to-day coordination, meeting logistics, documentation. Reports to steering committee. Specify decision-making rules: (1) Consensus decisions for major strategic choices (ensuring all members agree). (2) Majority voting for operational decisions (faster decision-making). (3) Steering committee veto power for decisions affecting member obligations. This tiered structure allows decision-making speed while ensuring no single member dominates.

keyPoints.title: Roles and Responsibilities
keyPoints.description: Clearly define roles to prevent role confusion and duplication. Steering Committee Chair (typically from anchor organization): Sets agenda, represents coalition externally, ensures members honor commitments. Steering Committee Members: Represent their organizations, provide resources and expertise, make decisions on behalf of their organizations. Working Group Leads: Organize meetings, manage deliverables, report progress to steering committee. Technical Lead: Provides specialized expertise, advises on technical feasibility. Civil Society Representative: Ensures equity, inclusion, and rights-centered perspective. Government Representative: Ensures policy alignment and resource availability. Private Sector Representative: Ensures implementation viability and market perspective. Operational Manager: Manages logistics, documentation, scheduling. Each role should have clear responsibilities and authority. Example: Technical Lead has authority to decide on technical standards within working group but must report decisions to steering committee for approval.

keyPoints.title: Meeting Cadence and Format
keyPoints.description: Coalitions require structured, regular engagement. Recommended cadence: (1) Steering Committee meetings: Monthly, 2 hours, hybrid format (allows virtual and in-person attendance). Agenda: decision items (30 min), progress reports (30 min), strategy/external relations (30 min), conflict resolution (30 min). (2) Working group meetings: Bi-weekly, 90 minutes. (3) Full coalition plenary: Quarterly or semi-annually, 4 hours, in-person if possible. Brings together all coalition members for alignment, celebration of milestones, stakeholder engagement. (4) Technical working group: Monthly, 2 hours. Meeting format matters. Distribute agenda in advance. Clarify decisions to be made vs. items for discussion. Use structured time (not open-ended discussion). Rotate meeting leadership to distribute ownership. Use virtual tools to allow remote participation. Document decisions and action items. Assign owners and deadlines. Circulate minutes within 48 hours. This structure transforms meetings from talk-shops into decision-making bodies that drive progress.

keyPoints.title: Communication Channels and Transparency
keyPoints.description: Coalition members need channels for information flow and coordination. Establish multiple channels: (1) Monthly coalition newsletter: Updates on progress, upcoming decisions, member highlights. Sent to all members and external stakeholders. Creates visibility and momentum. (2) Shared digital workspace: Collaborative platform (SharePoint, Google Drive, Asana) where documents, meeting notes, progress trackers live. All members can access, comment, and contribute. (3) Email list for steering committee: For time-sensitive decisions. (4) Slack or instant messaging: For working group coordination and quick questions. (5) Public communications: Website, social media, press releases for external stakeholders. Coalition communications serve multiple purposes: Internally, they ensure transparency and reduce information silos. Externally, they build awareness and credibility. Recommend quarterly external reporting: 'State of the Coalition' reports highlighting progress, challenges, and next steps. These reports should be publicly available, demonstrating transparency and building external support.

keyPoints.title: Conflict Resolution and Escalation
keyPoints.description: Coalition conflicts are inevitable. Establish clear escalation pathways. (1) Working group level: If two organizations disagree on technical approach, the working group lead facilitates discussion and seeks consensus. If consensus cannot be reached, escalate. (2) Steering committee level: Steering committee reviews the conflict, seeks input from both sides, makes a decision. The decision is binding. (3) External arbitration: For intractable conflicts, agree in advance on an external arbitrator (respected independent expert). In practice, most conflicts resolve at the working group level if there is skilled facilitation and clarity about the decision to be made. Prevent conflicts from festering by addressing them early. If a member misses commitments, address it directly within 1 week, not months later. If there is disagreement about coalition direction, surface it explicitly in steering committee meetings, not in side conversations. Clear escalation processes make conflict resolution faster and preserve relationships.

content.keyInsight: Coalition governance must reflect that the coalition is not a single organization but a network of independent organizations. Establish clear decision-making structures (steering committee, working groups, technical advisors), define roles and responsibilities, maintain regular meeting cadences, create multiple communication channels, and establish conflict resolution processes. Good governance enables fast decision-making while ensuring all members feel heard and valued.

exercises.prompt: Design the governance structure for a 12-member coalition building a national digital health infrastructure. Specify: (1) decision-making structure (committees, working groups, roles), (2) meeting cadence, (3) communication channels, (4) conflict resolution process.
Review a real multi-stakeholder coalition governance model (e.g., a published charter or governance document). What are the strengths? What governance gaps exist? How would you improve the structure?

content.overview: Coalitions are human systems, not mechanical systems. Managing coalition dynamics requires attention to trust, power, motivation, and morale. This module covers common coalition dynamics challenges: free-riding, power imbalances, mission creep, fatigue, and member turnover. These dynamics, if unmanaged, slowly erode coalition effectiveness.

keyPoints.title: Free-Riding and Contribution Accountability
keyPoints.description: In coalitions, some members contribute fully while others receive benefits without proportional contribution. A ministry might attend coalition meetings and offer vague support but contribute no budget or staff. This free-riding demoralizes contributors and undermines fairness. Address free-riding through: (1) Explicit contribution agreements. At coalition formation, specify each member's expected contributions: budget, staff hours, influence, access to constituencies. (2) Progress tracking and public reporting. In monthly steering committee meetings, review each member's progress toward commitments. Example: 'Ministry of Health committed to allocating 2 technical staff and 5 crore rupees. Current status: 1 staff allocated, 1 crore committed.' Public tracking creates accountability. (3) Tiered membership. If an organization cannot meet core commitments, they can downgrade to supporting membership with lower expectations. (4) Escalation to leadership. If a member organization consistently underperforms, escalate to their leadership (minister, CEO, director). Coalition leadership must be willing to have difficult conversations about contributions. Example: In India's Unique Digital Identity (Aadhaar) coalition, the Reserve Bank of India early on tracked each bank's integration progress and reported it publicly in steering meetings. Banks that lagged improved quickly—not from formal sanctions but from peer pressure and leadership attention. (5) Recognizing and celebrating contributors. Members who go above and beyond should be publicly recognized. This positive reinforcement encourages continued contribution.

keyPoints.title: Power Imbalances and Dominant Member Management
keyPoints.description: In many coalitions, one member is significantly more powerful than others (usually the anchor government ministry). If the powerful member dominates decision-making, other members become demotivated and disengaged. Manage power imbalances through: (1) Consensus-building on major decisions. Even if the powerful member could unilaterally decide, require consensus. This forces dialogue and ensures other voices are heard. (2) Structured participation in meetings. Use go-round formats where every member, regardless of size, gets air time. Use written input formats so smaller organizations can contribute even if less comfortable speaking up. (3) Rotating leadership. Rotate meeting facilitation, working group leadership, spokesperson roles among different coalition members. This distributes leadership and prevents dominance. (4) Explicit norms of respect for all voices. State clearly: 'In this coalition, a 50-person CSO has equal voting rights to a 50,000-person government ministry.' Put this in writing and reinforce it. (5) Separate working spaces. Smaller organizations can meet separately to develop positions before steering committee meetings. (6) External facilitation. If power imbalances create conflict, bring in external facilitators who can ensure inclusive dialogue. Example: In coalition building around data governance, smaller civil society organizations often felt unheard relative to government and tech companies. Creating a separate 'civil society strategy group' that met before larger coalition meetings allowed civil society to develop coherent positions and present them more effectively in the larger setting.

keyPoints.title: Mission Creep and Scope Management
keyPoints.description: Coalitions often drift from original scope. An identity coalition originally focused on financial inclusion gets asked to support health applications, education applications, legal services, etc. Scope expansion seems like success but actually overextends limited coalition resources and dilutes focus. Manage mission creep through: (1) Clear scope statement. The coalition charter explicitly defines what is in scope and what is out of scope. Example: 'This coalition's scope is building interoperable identity infrastructure. Applications (financial, health, legal) are outside our scope, though we build infrastructure they will use.' (2) Gatekeeping for new initiatives. Any new initiative must be approved by steering committee against the scope criteria. (3) Time-boxing explorations. If an out-of-scope area seems important, approve a limited exploration (3 months) to assess relevance. If relevant, formally expand scope through steering committee vote. If not relevant, mothball. (4) Sunset clauses. Any coalition initiative has an explicit end date. After that date, it stops unless explicitly renewed. This prevents indefinite scope creep. (5) Regular scope review. Quarterly, review the coalition's scope: Are we still focused on original objective? Have high-value new areas emerged that justify scope expansion? Is current scope overextended? Example: The Global Digital Compact started with focus on principles around digital governance. Over time, there was pressure to cover specific technology issues, specific regional problems, and specific company practices. By establishing clear scope boundaries, the coalition was able to stay focused while directing other issues to appropriate forums.

keyPoints.title: Fatigue and Motivation Management
keyPoints.description: Coalition work is draining. Members contribute without immediate institutional benefit. Meetings multiply. Bureaucracy increases. After 18-24 months, momentum slows, meetings have lower attendance, and engagement drops. This is normal but must be managed. Maintain motivation through: (1) Early wins. Achieve concrete results in the first 6 months. These might be small (published standards, successful pilot) but they demonstrate progress and momentum. (2) Celebration and recognition. Monthly celebrate progress. Quarterly hold all-hands meetings with external visibility. Annual hold larger recognition events. Make coalition work feel valued and visible. (3) Success stories. Document and communicate stories of impact. Example: 'This coalition's identity integration enabled a single mother to access 5 government benefits in 2 hours instead of 5 weeks.' These stories remind members why they joined. (4) Varied formats. Don't let all engagement be meetings and documents. Sponsor site visits, workshops, learning exchanges. Vary the modality to prevent monotony. (5) Leadership rotation. Rotating leadership roles (steering committee chair, spokesperson) keeps coalition leadership fresh and prevents burnout of individual leaders. (6) Explicit fatigue conversation. In steering committee meetings, ask: 'How is everyone's fatigue level? What can we do to make this less burdensome?' This explicit conversation often surfaces simple fixes (meet less frequently, shorter meetings, delegation to smaller groups). (7) Success metrics. Track and communicate progress toward coalition objectives. If members see the coalition is progressing toward stated goals, motivation is sustained. If progress stalls, motivation collapses. Track and communicate.

keyPoints.title: Member Transitions and Institutional Continuity
keyPoints.description: Coalition members change. A ministry officer leaves government. A CSO director takes a new role. A private sector partner merges with another company. These transitions can disrupt relationships and institutional knowledge. Manage transitions through: (1) Institutional rather than personal relationships. Build coalition relationships around organizational roles (the Ministry of Health's representative) rather than personal relationships (Rajesh Kumar). When Rajesh leaves, the ministry appoints a successor. The successor inherits the role and relationships. (2) Explicit successor planning. When a key coalition member signals they are leaving, ask them to identify and brief their successor 6-8 weeks before departure. (3) Documented institutional memory. Critical decisions, relationships, and history should be documented. A new member joining should be able to understand coalition history from documents, not just from conversations. (4) Onboarding process. When new organizations join or individuals change, have a structured onboarding: history briefing, relationship introductions, role clarity. This accelerates integration. (5) Continuity in key roles. Some roles (steering committee chair, technical lead) are high-impact. When these roles transition, ensure the transition is smooth with overlap between outgoing and incoming. Example: In a coalition, a long-serving steering committee chair stepped down. Rather than immediately replacing them, the coalition had a 3-month overlap where the new chair attended all meetings with the outgoing chair. The outgoing chair briefed them on upcoming decisions, member dynamics, and strategy. The new chair then led independently.

content.keyInsight: Coalition effectiveness depends on managing human dynamics: preventing free-riding through accountability, managing power imbalances through structural inclusion, controlling scope through gatekeeping, maintaining motivation through early wins and celebration, and ensuring continuity through institutional rather than personal relationships. Coalitions that attend to these dynamics sustain effort over years. Coalitions that neglect them slowly decay.

exercises.prompt: Consider a coalition that stalled or collapsed. Analyze: (1) What contributions were expected from members? Were they fulfilled? (2) Did power imbalances exist? How were they managed? (3) Did scope creep occur? (4) What was the motivation level trajectory? Why did it decline? (5) What would you have done differently?

Design a member engagement and motivation strategy for a 3-year coalition. Specify: (1) early wins that will build momentum, (2) celebration and recognition mechanisms, (3) success stories you will track and communicate, (4) strategies to prevent fatigue, (5) onboarding process for new members.

content.overview: Successful coalitions often need to grow: adding new members, expanding geographic scope, or deepening integration. Scaling requires different management approaches than startup. This module covers the mechanics of coalition expansion: when and how to add members, managing larger coalitions, geographic expansion, and preventing scaling breakdowns.

keyPoints.title: Adding Members and Concentric Scaling
keyPoints.description: Not all potential members should be added simultaneously. Use concentric circles of membership. (1) Inner core (5-8 organizations): Anchor and most committed partners. Meet monthly. Highest commitment. (2) Active members (8-15 organizations): Significant contributors but not core leadership. Meet monthly. (3) Supporting members (15-30 organizations): Benefit from coalition and provide input but lower commitment. Quarterly engagement. (4) Aligned organizations (30+): Support coalition goals but not formally part of governance. Annual engagement or public alignment. This structure allows growth without creating unwieldy meetings or decision-making gridlock. Add new members progressively: Start with core 5-8. After 6 months, add active members. After 12 months, add supporting members. After 18 months, open to aligned organizations. Vet new members against coalition criteria: Do they share coalition values? Do they have capacity to contribute? Do they bring unique perspectives or constituencies? Can they operate collaboratively? Recruit members through referral from existing members, not open calls. When recruiting, be explicit about the membership tier and what it entails. Example: India's payments coalition (RBI, banks, NPCI, government, fintech companies) operated for 2 years with core members before opening to a broader ecosystem of smaller fintech and service providers. This phased expansion allowed the coalition to establish norms and direction with a manageable size before scaling.

keyPoints.title: Geographic Expansion and Federated Coalitions
keyPoints.description: Coalitions often need to expand beyond a single location. A national digital initiative requires state-level coordination. An international initiative requires regional hubs. Manage geographic expansion through federation: (1) Central coalition: Establishes principles, standards, and overall direction. Meets quarterly or semi-annually. (2) Regional/state coalitions: Operate semi-autonomously within central coalition principles. Meet monthly locally. Coordinate with central coalition. Example: India's digital identity infrastructure (Aadhaar) has a central coalition at the federal level coordinating with state-level coalitions implementing in each state. (3) Harmonization meetings: Quarterly gatherings where regional representatives share learning, troubleshoot common issues, and maintain alignment. Prevent geographic expansion from creating fragmentation through: Strong center-setting principles and standards. Clear governance linking central and regional levels. Regular communication and harmonization. Empowering regional leadership (not micromanaging from center). Example: In a healthcare digital coalition expanding to 5 states, the central coalition establishes: (a) Data interoperability standards all states must follow, (b) Privacy and security requirements, (c) Governance principles. Each state's coalition then operates its own rollout, member recruitment, and implementation within these parameters. Quarterly harmonization calls bring together all state leads to share learning and address gaps.

keyPoints.title: Preventing Scaling Breakdown and Fragmentation
keyPoints.description: A common scaling failure: as coalitions grow, they fragment into subgroups, lose coherence, and stop functioning as a unified entity. Prevent this through: (1) Maintaining clear coalition identity and purpose. As the coalition grows, explicitly reinforce core identity: 'We are the Coalition for Open Government Data. Our purpose is making government data accessible to citizens and businesses.' This becomes more important as the coalition grows. (2) Strong governance at scale. At 10 members, loose governance works. At 50 members, loose governance creates chaos. As the coalition scales, governance must become more structured (clearer roles, more explicit decision-making rules, professional coordination). (3) Specialized working groups. Rather than expecting all members to participate in all decisions, create working groups for specific areas (technical standards, communications, policy, implementation). This allows scaling without requiring all members to attend all meetings. (4) Tiered communication. At small size, all members can receive all information. At scale, create targeted communications: core members get detailed updates, active members get quarterly summaries, supporting members get annual reports. (5) Professional coordination. At 5 members, a part-time coordinator suffices. At 20 members, you need professional staff managing coordination. As coalitions scale, add professional management. (6) Regular refocusing exercises. Annually, step back and ask: Are we still focused on our core objective? Have we drifted? Do we need to refocus or explicitly expand scope? Coalitions that scale successfully maintain strong identity despite growth.

keyPoints.title: Deepening Integration Within Coalition
keyPoints.description: Scaling is not just adding members; it is deepening how members work together. As coalitions mature, move from parallel action to integrated action. (1) Parallel action phase (months 1-12): Each member works on their piece independently but coordinates with others. Example: Banks independently integrate with central identity system. Integration is technical coordination only. (2) Integrated action phase (months 12+): Members coordinate deeply on strategy, shared resources, and joint problem-solving. Example: Banks jointly set interoperability standards, jointly troubleshoot integration issues, jointly train staff. This deepening requires: Increased trust (takes time to develop). Formal integration mechanisms (working groups, task forces, joint committees). Shared resources (sometimes members contribute staff to joint teams). Clear governance allowing integrated decision-making. Example: The Global Fund's coalition of donors, NGOs, countries, and private sector moved from parallel funding and programs (each organization implementing separately) to integrated country-level strategies (all organizations coordinating around country-specific plans). This deepening increased effectiveness but required more sophisticated governance and trust.

content.keyInsight: Scale coalitions through concentric circles of membership (core, active, supporting, aligned) rather than trying to onboard everyone at once. Manage geographic expansion through federation while maintaining strong central principles. Prevent fragmentation by maintaining clear identity, strengthening governance, creating specialized working groups, and adding professional management. Deepen integration over time by moving from parallel action to joint strategy and shared resources.

exercises.prompt: Your coalition is expanding from 8 core members to 40 organizations. Design: (1) concentric membership structure, (2) governance changes needed for scale, (3) working group structure, (4) communication strategy for different tiers, (5) timeline and triggers for each scaling phase.

Your government is expanding a digital initiative from one state to all 10 states. Design a federated coalition structure: (1) central coalition role and membership, (2) state coalition role and membership, (3) governance linking central and state, (4) harmonization mechanisms, (5) how you would prevent fragmentation.

content.overview: Coalitions built around a specific initiative often collapse once the initiative ends. A coalition that built a digital identity system disbands after launch. A coalition that improved government data access breaks apart once initial policies are set. Sustainable coalitions transcend specific projects and become institutional features. This module covers the mechanics of coalition sustainability: transforming project-based coalitions into institution coalitions, managing transitions from founder leadership, creating self-sustaining incentives, and succession planning.

keyPoints.title: From Project to Institution Transformation
keyPoints.description: Many coalitions are organized around a specific project: 'Build and launch digital identity system.' Once the project launches, the coalition's purpose seems complete. The coalition then either disbands or becomes rudderless. Transform project-based coalitions into institutional coalitions by (1) Expanding the mission beyond initial project. Original mission: 'Launch digital identity system.' Expanded mission: 'Build and sustain secure, accessible digital identity infrastructure serving citizens and government.' This expanded mission includes post-launch responsibilities (operating the system, extending to new use cases, maintaining security, ensuring equity). (2) Establishing multi-phase objectives. Phase 1 (months 1-24): Launch digital identity. Phase 2 (months 24-48): Expand to 5 new use cases. Phase 3 (months 48-60): Ensure long-term sustainability and security. This multi-phase approach gives the coalition continuing purpose. (3) Creating standing institutions. Rather than disbanding, transform the coalition into a standing body with permanent or rolling 3-5 year mandates. Example: Instead of 'Task Force to Build Digital Identity System' (temporary), establish 'Digital Identity Authority Coalition' (standing body). (4) Demonstrating ongoing value. Coalitions persist when they continue delivering value to members. Post-launch, demonstrate value through: operating efficiency gains, new use cases enabled, equity improvements, cost savings. Constantly communicate this value to members. (5) Securing institutional funding. Project-based coalitions rely on project funding. As projects end, funding ends. Institutional coalitions need institutional funding sources. Examples: government core budget allocation, sector fees, multi-donor funding. Example: India's UPI coalition started as a project to build and launch UPI. As UPI succeeded, the coalition transformed into the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), an institution. NPCI continues evolving the UPI system, adding features, and coordinating stakeholders. The coalition transformed into a standing institution.

keyPoints.title: Founder Leadership Transition
keyPoints.description: Most coalitions have a founding leader (often a charismatic government official or respected external expert). This leader provides initial vision, convenes members, and drives early momentum. If the coalition becomes dependent on this individual, it cannot sustain beyond their tenure. Prepare for founder transition through: (1) Early documentation of vision and philosophy. The founder should document the coalition's core principles, decision-making philosophy, and approach. This becomes reference material for successors. (2) Leadership development in others. From year 1, develop other leaders within the coalition. Rotate responsibilities. Have founders mentor potential successors. By the time the founder leaves, multiple capable leaders have emerged. (3) Institutional roles, not individual authority. Define the steering committee chair role (not attach it to one person's leadership). Define the strategic director role. Define the spokesperson role. This allows leadership to transition as people change. (4) Explicit succession planning. As a founder approaches transition (change of role, retirement, etc.), initiate formal succession process: 1-2 years before transition, identify internal candidates. Coach candidates for 6-12 months. Transition with 6-month overlap. After transition, maintain relationship with founder as advisor. (5) Institutional memory beyond the founder. Document key decisions, relationships, and history. When new leadership arrives, they inherit both role and context. (6) Distributed leadership model. Rather than founder as sole leader, establish distributed model: steering committee collectively provides leadership, rotating spokesperson role, technical and strategic advisors separate from operations. Example: India's Aadhaar program was strongly identified with Nandan Nilekani in its founding phase. To sustain beyond his tenure, the Reserve Bank of India gradually built institutional capacity, developed other leaders, documented principles, and by Nilekani's departure, the Unique Identification Authority (UIDAI) functioned as an independent institution not dependent on a single leader.

keyPoints.title: Self-Sustaining Incentives and Benefit Streams
keyPoints.description: Coalitions persist when members benefit from continued membership. (1) Direct benefit streams: Members receive concrete value from coalition. Examples: Banks benefit from increased transaction volume from UPI. Government benefits from improved service delivery. Civil society benefits from increased citizen inclusion. Continuously demonstrate and expand these benefit streams. (2) Network effects: Membership provides access to expanding network of peers, learnings, best practices. As coalition grows, network becomes more valuable. Communicate these network effects. (3) Reputation and visibility: Coalition provides members visibility and reputation. Award recognition, speaking opportunities, celebration of successful members. (4) Standards and interoperability: Coalition defines standards that allow members' systems to work together. Members benefit from interoperability. As interoperability deepens, leaving becomes costly. (5) Risk sharing: Coalition helps members share risks. When risks are distributed across coalition, individual members face lower risk. (6) Market access: For private sector members, coalition provides market access. Once coalition has critical mass, market presence attracts new companies. Sustain self-interest through: constantly demonstrating member benefits, expanding coalition benefits over time, ensuring equitable benefit distribution (free-riders don't persist), celebrating member success. Example: India's fintech payments coalition (UPI) sustains member participation through: transactional volume increasing (banks benefit), cost per transaction decreasing (merchants benefit), financial inclusion expanding (government benefits), new use cases emerging (technology companies benefit). These aligned benefit streams keep members engaged.

keyPoints.title: Evolution and Adaptation Over Time
keyPoints.description: Sustainable coalitions adapt as context changes. A coalition built around a specific technology must adapt as technology evolves. A coalition built around specific policy must adapt as policy evolves. (1) Regular strategic reviews: Annually, assess: Are we still focused on core mission? Has context changed? Do we need to adapt approach? (2) Flexibility within core principles: Coalition has non-negotiable core principles (e.g., 'financial inclusion is central'). Within these principles, coalition adapts tactics. Early phase: focus on rural penetration. Later phase: focus on urban convenience. Same principle, adapted tactics. (3) Member feedback and evolution: Solicit member input regularly: 'What should the coalition evolve toward?' Incorporate member feedback into strategy. This keeps the coalition aligned with member needs. (4) External learning: Scan global landscape for emerging practices. When relevant, adapt coalition practices. Example: If a different country's coalition solved a problem elegantly, learn and adapt. (5) Sunsetting and renewal: Some coalition initiatives naturally end (e.g., 'achieve 10 million users' is completed). Celebrate completion, then sunset the initiative. Don't let completed initiatives become zombie projects consuming time and energy. (6) Welcoming new members and perspectives: As the coalition evolves, new types of members become relevant. Welcome them. New perspectives prevent stagnation. Example: India's Aadhaar coalition, which started focused on financial inclusion, evolved to incorporate health, education, and legal applications. Civil society skeptics were early critics. Over time, many became coalition members, deepening equity focus. The coalition evolved to incorporate new stakeholder types without losing core identity. Example: OpenGov partnership started as a coalition of reformers focused on getting governments to release data. As it evolved, it incorporated private sector interested in using data, developed capacity-building components, and shifted from pure openness advocacy to pragmatic implementation. This evolution kept the coalition relevant.

content.keyInsight: Coalition sustainability requires transforming project-based initiatives into institutional roles, planning for founder leadership transition through distributed leadership and succession planning, creating self-sustaining incentive structures where members continuously benefit from membership, and enabling evolution to remain relevant as context changes. Sustainable coalitions transcend specific projects and become standing features of institutional landscapes.

exercises.prompt: You are managing a coalition that has successfully launched a digital initiative. Design a sustainability strategy: (1) Transform the project mission into institution mission. (2) Develop a 3-phase roadmap (launch phase complete, what are next 5-year phases?). (3) Plan for founder's departure in 24 months. Develop leadership succession. (4) Identify member benefit streams and how you would deepen them. (5) Design annual strategic review process. (6) Identify potential evolution areas (what new challenges might the coalition tackle).

Analyze a coalition that collapsed or stalled after initial success (or one you know that sustained). What enabled or prevented sustainability? Evaluate: (1) Was it transformed from project to institution? (2) Was founder transition managed? (3) Were member benefits sustained? (4) Did the coalition evolve? What would you have done differently?
